blogs.title: Through the Wild Lens of Royalty: Shivanjali Kumari Dungarpur
blogs.subtitle: Princess Shivanjali Kumari Dungarpur on patience, the Masai Mara and a royal inheritance reimagined through the lens. A Portraits of Excellence profile.
blogs.content:
Princess Shivanjali Kumari Dungarpur — where the weight of an ancient lineage meets the fearless eye of a modern artist.

In the lake city of Dungarpur, where heritage and wilderness have always shared the same horizon, Shivanjali Kumari has built a practice of quiet, extraordinary attention. A princess by birthright, a wildlife photographer by conviction, she moves through the wild with the patience of someone who understands that the most powerful images are never taken — they are waited for. Her lens captures not merely the animals of Rajasthan's forests and wetlands, but the emotional grammar of the natural world: stillness before the hunt, the tenderness between a cheetah and her cubs, the dignity of creatures entirely indifferent to the human gaze. Each frame is a testament to her belief that photography, at its finest, is an act of profound respect.

On the ancient lakes of Dungarpur, where Pareva stone glows blue-grey in the morning light and every ripple carries the memory of a dynasty — she waits, watches, and finds her frame.
◆
Chapter I

The City That Made Her

The hilly terrain of southern Rajasthan cradles Dungarpur — a city of Pareva stone that glows bluish-grey in dawn light, of palaces that have outlasted dynasties. It is from this soil that Shivanjali Kumari Dungarpur — nineteen, princess by birthright, photographer by passion — draws her vision of the world.

Most who inherit a royal lineage inherit its rituals. Shivanjali inherited its gaze. The seven-storey Juna Mahal; the serene Udai Bilas Palace, her family's seat and today a celebrated heritage hotel. These are not backdrops to her life but the grammar of her artistic language — one she now speaks through a camera, studying at Le Mark Institute in Bombay.

◆
Chapter II

A Lockdown and an iPhone 5

Her journey began not in a studio but in the stillness of a lockdown. In 2020 her school, Mayo College, encouraged entry to a Round Square Conference on the arts. Armed only with an iPhone 5, she submitted her work — and emerged first runner-up across all-India. She returned transformed, earning her photography badge and rising to official Head Photographer, a role that pulled her from mid-lecture to capture school life as it happened.

“Nature has its own pace — it is raw, wild, and not performing for humans. This is the lesson I carry from every safari, every hour before sunrise, every quiet moment in the field.”

— Shivanjali Kumari Dungarpur
Chapter III

The Most Powerful Permission

By the middle of twelfth grade the decision was made: photography, and nothing else. Her parents offered the most powerful of permissions — “If you love it so much, why not?” For a young woman navigating expectations woven into centuries of royal heritage, it was an act of liberation. She enrolled in her degree with the blessing of a family that chose to celebrate her art over convention.

Chapter IV

Where Philosophy Met Craft

Wildlife photography became the domain where philosophy met craft. She speaks of early safaris at Jim Corbett — frustrating hours, no sightings — and the eventual grace of patience; of the Masai Mara, where a lion at rest became a meditation on authenticity. She begins each photograph with a quiet intent, forming the core emotion before pressing the shutter.

Her most personal photograph remains a cheetah and her cubs in the Masai Mara. The cheetah, guides warned, is the rarest of the great cats to find. After ten drives, rising at four each morning, she found nothing. She held her instincts close — and on one of her last drives the cheetah walked into her frame as though always meant to. It holds everything she believes about patience and conviction.

The Portfolio · Masai Mara

Plates I–III

Chapter V

Other Inheritances

Beyond the wild she carries other inheritances: a bond with her father through automobiles, preserved in the family's car museum at Dungarpur, where a vintage Jaguar's lines echo the precision she seeks through her lens. From her mother, Her Highness Priyadarshini Kumari Dungarpur — who carried Rajasthani cuisine to Switzerland in 1991 — came a fascination with baking, and a diploma at Sophia College.

The Tabla & The Shutter
“I played the tabla for ten years. I made a promise to my late grandfather to continue. It brings rhythm to my visual life — the beat of my hands and the click of the shutter, two instruments in the same pursuit of truth.”
— Shivanjali Kumari Dungarpur
Chapter VI

An Inheritance, Reimagined

After graduation her path is clear: study abroad, then commit fully to wildlife photography — chasing the unscripted, the unheld, the real. Alongside the camera, the tabla continues, in honour of a grandfather's memory.

She does not photograph to perform. She photographs to understand — the cheetah in the grass, the palace at first light, the city that made her. In her hands a camera is not merely a tool. It is an inheritance, reimagined.

At A Glance · FAQ

Questions & Lineage

Who is Shivanjali Kumari Dungarpur?
A nineteen-year-old wildlife photographer and princess of Dungarpur, Rajasthan, studying at Le Mark Institute in Bombay.

What is her most personal photograph?
A cheetah and her cubs in the Masai Mara, found on one of her last drives after ten mornings of searching.

Where is her family's seat?
Udai Bilas Palace in Dungarpur, today a celebrated heritage hotel.

blogs.title: Dining Like Royalty: The Culinary Legacy of India's Palaces
blogs.subtitle: The royal kitchens of India — Awadhi, Hyderabadi, Rajasthani and Mewari traditions born in palace kitchens — and how they survive on contemporary tables.
blogs.content:
The most refined cooking in India was not born in restaurants but in the kitchens of its palaces. From Awadhi dum pukht to Hyderabadi biryani, the royal table defined what the subcontinent considered luxurious — and much of it can still be tasted today.

The Royal Kitchen: Where Indian Cuisine Was Refined

Every great cuisine has an aristocracy, and India's was its royal kitchens. For centuries, the palaces of the subcontinent maintained kitchens of extraordinary scale and refinement — staffed by hereditary cooks, supplied by the best of every region, and governed by a single obsession: that the table of a king should be unlike any other.

The royal kitchen was a laboratory of technique. It is here that slow cooking reached its most exacting form, that spices were balanced to a precision ordinary households never attempted, and that presentation was elevated from serving to ceremony. A royal banquet was not merely a meal; it was a statement of power, hospitality and discernment, in which the quality of the food was inseparable from the authority of the host.

What survives today is more than a collection of recipes. It is a set of culinary traditions — each tied to a particular court, a particular region and a particular idea of what luxury tastes like — that together constitute the most sophisticated cooking India has produced.

Awadhi and Hyderabadi: Two Schools of Refinement

The two most celebrated royal cuisines of India are the products of two very different courts. Awadhi cuisine, from Lucknow, is the cooking of the Nawabs of Awadh — famous for the dum pukht technique, in which ingredients are sealed in a pot and cooked slowly over a low flame so that flavours deepen without escaping. It produced the refined kebabs, the delicate gravies and the fragrant biryanis that define North Indian courtly food.

Hyderabadi cuisine, by contrast, carries the influence of the Deccan's Persian and Central Asian connections, filtered through the kitchens of the Nizam. Its signature is the Hyderabadi biryani — layered rice and meat, seasoned with saffron and slow-steamed — and a tradition of rich, carefully spiced dishes that reflect centuries of culinary exchange at one of India's wealthiest courts.

Between them, Awadh and Hyderabad established the principle that has governed Indian luxury cooking ever since: that refinement is not the addition of richness but the control of it. Restraint, timing and balance — not mere extravagance — are what separate the royal table from the merely generous one.

“Refinement is not the addition of richness but the control of it.”

On the discipline of royal cooking

Rajasthani and Mewari: The Cuisine of the Desert Courts

If Awadh and Hyderabad refined richness, the royal kitchens of Rajasthan mastered something harder: abundance in a landscape of scarcity. The desert courts of the Rajputs produced a cooking of extraordinary character, built for a climate where ingredients were limited and preservation was essential.

Rajasthani royal cuisine is often remembered for its heat and its game — laal maas, the fiery red mutton curry of the Rajput kitchens, is its most famous export — but its true sophistication lies elsewhere: in the ingenuity of dishes that used dried ingredients, dairy and spice to create depth where fresh produce was scarce. Mewari cuisine, from the court of Mewar around Udaipur, shares that foundation while developing its own register of sweet-savoury balance and festive thalis.

To dine at one of Rajasthan's palace hotels today is to encounter this tradition intact — served in dining rooms that once fed the court, and prepared by kitchens that trace their methods to the households of the Maharanas. It is history that can be tasted.

“It is history that can be tasted.”

On dining at Rajasthan's palace hotels

How the Royal Table Survives Today

The question of how these cuisines have survived is answered, in large part, by the same institutions that preserved the palaces themselves. The palace hotels of India did not only save the buildings; they saved the kitchens. Hereditary cooks and their recipes passed into the employment of heritage properties, where the cooking of the courts continues to be served, adapted and studied.

At the same time, the traditions have moved outward. Chefs trained in these kitchens have carried the techniques into India's fine-dining restaurants and into the international understanding of Indian food. Dishes that were once the privilege of a court are now made in home kitchens across the country, their origins gradually forgotten even as their flavour endures.

For the contemporary diner, this presents an opportunity. To eat Awadhi food in Lucknow, Hyderabadi food in Hyderabad, or a royal Rajasthani thali in a restored palace, is to taste something that has passed through centuries of refinement — a direct, sensory connection to the courts that created it.

The Royal Gallerys Perspective

THE ROYAL GALLERYS treats cuisine as part of the same heritage we document everywhere else — not as a sidebar to the palaces, but as one of the most immediate ways their culture remains alive. A royal recipe is an archive in edible form, carrying decisions about technique, ingredients and hospitality across generations.

For the traveller, the royal table offers the rare chance to consume heritage directly rather than merely observe it. For the restaurants, hotels and chefs who carry these traditions forward, it offers a provenance that no marketing campaign can manufacture.

blogs.title: The Balmoral: Three Minutes Ahead of Edinburgh
blogs.subtitle: Inside Edinburgh's landmark railway hotel at No. 1 Princes Street. Architecture, Palm Court, suites, and a century of Scottish heritage.
blogs.content:
For more than a century the clock above Waverley has run fast on purpose. Inside Edinburgh’s great railway hotel, a house fluent in both Old Town and New.

The clock above Waverley has been three minutes fast since 1902, so that nobody hurrying up from the platforms should miss a train. It is a civic courtesy engineered in gilded cast iron: three minutes granted to human hesitation, to luggage straps, to farewells spoken under steam. For one hundred and twenty-four years, the only night the clock is permitted to keep true Greenwich time is Hogmanay—the thirty-first of December—when Edinburgh counts down together before the bells, and fiction gives way to the real midnight.

Arrive as the hotel was meant to be arrived at, by rail, and the city sorts itself in a single movement: the Old Town’s volcanic ridge climbing precipitously to the south, Princes Street running west in Georgian order, and above you fifty-eight metres of Scottish sandstone holding the Northern sky. To step off the train and ascend directly into No. 1 Princes Street is to experience the Victorian railway hotel at its zenith—not as an escape from the city, but as its threshold.

The Details

The Balmoral, a Rocco Forte Hotel

Address: 1 Princes Street, Edinburgh EH2 2EQ, Scotland

Contact: +44 131 556 2414 · roccofortehotels.com

Opened: 15 October 1902 · Listing: Category B (1994)

Architect: William Hamilton Beattie (completed by Andrew Robb Scott) · Interiors: Olga Polizzi

A landmark in time

The hotel was conceived as an instrument of arrival. In the closing decade of the nineteenth century, the North British Railway sought an imposing monument worthy of its rebuilt subterranean station. The established hoteliers of Princes Street, alarmed by the scale and audacity of the railway company’s ambition, fought the scheme fiercely before a committee of the House of Lords. They lost.

The architectural competition of 1895 went to William Hamilton Beattie, the accomplished architect responsible for Jenners department store further along the street. Beattie drew a grand palace of Victorian Scottish Baronial drama, but fate intervened: he died in 1898. His capable assistant Andrew Robb Scott took up the drawings and carried the vast building through four further years of masonry and finishing to its opening on 15 October 1902.

It opened as the North British Station Hotel, serving generations of travellers arriving from King’s Cross on the Flying Scotsman. Renamed The Balmoral in 1991, the property has been a Rocco Forte hotel since 1997, and has held Category B listed status since 1994.

“The greatest luxury at this address is not a room. It is a fixed point from which a moving city becomes legible.”

The architecture: fluent in two Edinburghs

The façade is sandstone cut from the beds that built the Georgian terraces, but darker and deeper in section, modelled for shadow rather than line. The stone holds rain the way the Old Town does, so the building is rarely the colour it was an hour ago. In morning drizzle it turns the tone of wet tweed; under late afternoon sun through the Firth of Forth, it glows amber against the basalt crags.

The tower’s four great dials were made by the historic Edinburgh horologists Hamilton & Inches, whose George Street workshops still maintain the mechanism. On three hundred and sixty-four days each year, those hands register three minutes before the hour, keeping Edinburgh’s travelers impeccably punctual.

Inside: Palm Court and the suites

The door is at No. 1 Princes Street. The plan turns inward and upward (marble, galleries, stairs) towards Palm Court: palms rising between fluted columns beneath a glass dome, a Venetian chandelier, and a hand-painted de Gournay landscape in which the follies of Calton Hill are hidden among the trees. Afternoons bring a harpist, and tea is poured from a table of eighty-eight leaves.

Interiors are by Olga Polizzi, Sir Rocco’s sister and the group’s director of design. Fabrics carry the landscape: blues, greys and moss-greens, and a tartan woven for the house rather than borrowed from a clan. The Scone & Crombie Suite, named for Scone Palace and Crombie Castle, is a hundred and twenty square metres above the Old Town, with a powder-blue overmantel of carved garlands and gilt sconces flanking the glass.

Food and drink

Brasserie Prince, remade in 2018 by Martin Brudnizki with Olga Polizzi, was given its own door onto Princes Street. Downstairs, Number One provides the hotel’s formal fine-dining stage, framed by lacquered walls and contemporary art. Across the entrance hall, SCOTCH presents an amber library of more than five hundred single malts, blends, and rare vintages, tended by kilted Whisky Ambassadors.

The spa

The spa below was rebuilt as the first Irene Forte Spa in the country, with lemon-tree frescoes and cork underfoot. The subterranean sanctuary houses a fifteen-metre heated lap pool, steam rooms, and restorative treatment suites where Mediterranean botanicals meet Scottish tranquillity.

The service and the tartan

The Balmoral tartan was made for the hotel by the Edinburgh kiltmakers Kinloch Anderson, and is worn in kilt and in trews. In an era when hotel uniforms often lean towards global uniformity, the sight of doormen greeting arrivals at the foot of Princes Street in bespoke kilt and tailored wool asserts an unapologetic sense of place.

Literary Edinburgh

Waverley takes its name from Scott’s novels; in 2004 Edinburgh became the first UNESCO City of Literature. In January 2007, in a room upstairs, J.K. Rowling finished the last of the Harry Potter novels, signing the marble bust in Room 552—now preserved as the J.K. Rowling Suite—before closing a defining chapter in modern English fiction.

“Grand hotels ask to be admired. This one asks what time you are leaving, and quietly sees to it that you are not late.”

The neighbourhood

Step out of the front door and Edinburgh arranges itself into four directions, none longer than a walk: west along Princes Street to the National; south across North Bridge up to the Old Town and the Castle; east to Calton Hill; north to George Street and the workshops of Hamilton & Inches.

Know before you go

  • Arrival by rail: Lift and staircase access connects directly from the Edinburgh Waverley Station concourse to No. 1 Princes Street.
  • The clock tower: Calibrated three minutes fast throughout the year; the only night it reflects Greenwich Mean Time is Hogmanay (31 December).
  • Afternoon Tea: Served daily in Palm Court beneath the glass dome; reservations for the afternoon harpist sittings should be secured well in advance.
  • Room selection: Classic courtyard rooms offer nineteen square metres of secluded quiet; deluxe Castle-view rooms measure twenty-eight square metres and frame direct vistas of the fortress.
  • Staff tartan: Tailored exclusively for the hotel by Kinloch Anderson, Scotland’s premier kiltmakers since 1868.
